entry.title: How Argonne Is Making Nuclear Fuel Recycling Equipment 50 Times Smaller

media:group.media:title: How Argonne Is Making Nuclear Fuel Recycling Equipment 50 Times Smaller
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. With expertise in chemical separations, nuclear fuel recycling and critical materials recovery, Argonne is developing technologies that could make recovering valuable materials more efficient and cost-effective through research supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E).
Recycling used nuclear fuel requires separating valuable materials from complex mixtures, a process that traditionally depends on large, costly equipment. Conventional separation systems can require substantial space, shielding and inventories of solvents and other materials, particularly when handling radioactive substances. These requirements increase operating costs and waste generation, creating barriers to deploying fuel recycling technologies at commercial scale.
To address these challenges, Argonne and Case Western Reserve University are developing PACERS, compact centrifugal equipment for radiochemical separations. Using rapidly spinning packed beds, the technology generates centrifugal forces hundreds of times greater than gravity to intensify mixing and material separation. In demonstrations, a PACERS solvent extraction unit achieved more than 50 times smaller equipment volume than conventional mixer-settlers at the same process throughput, with mass transfer improvements of tenfold or greater. A related ion exchange system doubled rare earth capture capacity using a standard adsorbent compared with a conventional resin bed.
By delivering separation performance in a much smaller package, PACERS could reduce the shielding, solvents, adsorbents and other materials needed for nuclear fuel recycling, lowering costs and reducing waste. The technology also has potential applications beyond nuclear energy, including recovering critical materials from coal ash and mining waste. Together, these advances could help make valuable material recovery more practical, efficient and economically viable.

entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Argonne Brings Agentic AI to X-ray Science

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Argonne Brings Agentic AI to X-ray Science
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, researchers demonstrate how SYNAPS-I, a cross-facility effort under DOE’s Genesis Mission, is bringing artificial intelligence directly into experiments at the Advanced Photon Source (APS).
Advanced X-ray facilities such as the APS give researchers powerful tools for imaging and understanding materials at extremely small scales. But conducting these experiments can require scientists to navigate complex controls, analyze large amounts of data and make decisions about where to measure next. These demands can slow experiments and create a steep learning curve for researchers who are less familiar with synchrotron facilities and beamline controls.
SYNAPS-I is working to change that by combining AI foundation models with agentic tools that can analyze experimental data and interact directly with beamline systems. At the Center for Nanoscale Materials’ hard X-ray nanoprobe beamline at the APS, researchers demonstrated an AI agent that allows users to perform routine actions through natural-language instructions rather than writing code or navigating complex control interfaces. AI can also help identify features of interest in incoming data and automate processes that have traditionally required human decision-making, giving researchers feedback while an experiment is still underway.
The work is part of a broader collaboration across U.S. Department of Energy light and neutron sources. SYNAPS-I demonstrations have been performed at the Advanced Light Source at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne and the National Synchrotron Light Source II at Brookhaven National Laboratory, with future demonstrations expected to expand to additional DOE facilities. By combining data and expertise across facilities, researchers are working toward AI tools that can support a wider scientific user community.
Ultimately, these capabilities could make advanced experiments more efficient and accessible while allowing scientists to spend less time on routine tasks and more time interpreting results and pursuing important scientific questions. The work supports DOE’s Genesis Mission goal of using AI to increase the productivity and impact of U.S. science and technology.

entry.title: Operations in Action: Keeping Argonne Cool

media:group.media:title: Operations in Action: Keeping Argonne Cool
media:group.media:description:
Every day, Argonne depends on hundreds of millions of gallons of cooling water to keep its buildings, equipment, and research infrastructure operating. Behind that effort is the laboratory's canal water treatment plant, where operators, mechanics, and engineers work around the clock to provide a reliable supply of treated water that helps make world-class science possible.
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where teams work together to solve complex scientific and technical challenges. Supporting that mission depends on reliable infrastructure, including the systems that provide the cooling water essential to research, high-performance computing, and facility operations.
As Argonne's scientific capabilities continue to grow, so does the demand for cooling water. The canal water treatment plant processes hundreds of millions of gallons of water each year, with demand increasing as new research facilities and high-performance computing resources come online. Meeting those needs requires a dependable system with the capacity to support the laboratory today while preparing for tomorrow.
Drawing water from a nearby canal, the team removes suspended solids through a carefully managed treatment process before distributing the water throughout the site for cooling. After serving its purpose, the water is returned to the Des Plaines River cleaner than when it entered the treatment plant. Keeping this nearly 60-year-old system operating requires the expertise of skilled operators, mechanics, and engineers who maintain equipment, monitor water quality, and continually improve the system to meet the laboratory's evolving needs.
Providing this essential service requires dedicated professionals working every day of the year—including nights, weekends, and holidays—to ensure Argonne's operations never miss a beat. Their work demonstrates that innovation extends beyond the laboratory bench, relying on the expertise, teamwork, and commitment of operations professionals whose efforts make scientific discovery possible.

media:group.media:title: Argonne OutLoud: The Next Frontier: How AI Is Reshaping Discovery at Argonne
media:group.media:description:
9/17/2026 – Sean L. Jones, Mike Papka, Ilke Arslan, Ravi Madduri
This edition of Argonne National Laboratory’s OutLoud Public Lecture Series focuses on The Next Frontier: How AI Is Reshaping Discovery at Argonne, with researchers discussing how AI is contributing to advancements in discovery.
Hear from experts in the world of cosmology, autonomous discovery and biomedical research who explain how they’re using AI to get further, faster. Long before “artificial intelligence” was a household term, Argonne was building the machines and concepts that would make it possible.
This OutLoud lecture turns the spotlight on Argonne’s AI story — where it started, where it stands today, and where it’s headed as part of a bold new national mission tackling America’s toughest scientific challenges using AI. The collaborative effort among the national laboratory complex, U.S. Department of Energy, and private sector is known as Genesis Mission.
This lecture offers a full circle look at Argonne’s AI story: how building a 1950s computer to solve nuclear physics problems, fostered the roots of artificial intelligence and automated reasoning.

In this episode, Sibendu Som, director of Argonne’s Materials Manufacturing Innovation Center and AI Applications Initiative, explains how large language models and agentic AI are changing his everyday workflow. Som uses AI to help summarize and review proposals, allowing him to work through information much faster while keeping human expertise and critical judgment at the center of the process.
Som also introduces AISAC, an AI scientific co-assistant developed at Argonne that can help users select the right AI models for different tasks, including working with documents, spreadsheets and code. His advice for getting started with AI is simple: experiment with it and learn where it can make you more effective.

In this episode, Valerie Taylor, director of Argonne’s Mathematics and Computer Science Division, discusses how AI is changing the scale and speed of her research. Taylor and her colleagues use AI for tasks ranging from data analysis and code generation to simultaneously exploring software and hardware designs. In one example, about 150 AI agents work in parallel, allowing researchers to explore 150 designs in the time it would traditionally take to explore one.
Taylor has worked with AI for more than a decade, while researchers in her division have been advancing AI methods for more than 30 years. Her perspective on today’s rapid advances is clear: AI isn’t about replacing scientists. It’s about complementing their expertise and helping them use their time more productively.

entry.title: 90,000 Tons of Used Nuclear Fuel. Now What? Argonne Is Working on an Answer

media:group.media:title: 90,000 Tons of Used Nuclear Fuel. Now What? Argonne Is Working on an Answer
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. With decades of expertise in nuclear fuel cycles and pyroprocessing, Argonne is advancing technologies that could help recover valuable energy-generating materials from used nuclear fuel through research supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E).
The United States has more than 90,000 tons of used nuclear fuel in storage, much of which still contains energy-generating materials that could potentially be recovered. But used fuel leaves a reactor as a stable oxide, and before it can be recycled through pyroprocessing, that oxide must first be converted into a metallic form. Moving this process toward commercial scale requires researchers to overcome challenges in efficiency, cost and the ability to monitor the conversion as it happens.
To address these challenges, Argonne researchers and their partners are advancing electrochemical oxide reduction, the first step in preparing used oxide fuel for pyroprocessing. The team is developing real-time sensors to track the conversion from oxide to metal, evaluating next-generation alternatives to expensive anode materials, and working with Case Western Reserve University to model an improved cell design that could increase electrochemical efficiency.
The project also looks beyond the conversion process to the broader nuclear fuel cycle. Oklo Inc. is evaluating the used fuel supply that could serve as feedstock for the process, while Deep Isolation is developing disposal strategies for the material that remains. Together, the partners are working toward a more complete pathway from used nuclear fuel to new advanced reactor fuel and, ultimately, final waste disposal.
Advancing oxide reduction could help remove a key barrier to scaling pyroprocessing and supporting future advanced reactors. By recovering energy-generating materials from used fuel, this approach could reduce the need to mine new uranium, strengthen the domestic nuclear fuel supply and help transform used nuclear fuel from a long-term challenge into a strategic energy resource.

entry.title: Making Used Nuclear Fuel Less Permanent

media:group.media:title: Making Used Nuclear Fuel Less Permanent
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. With expertise in accelerator technology, reactor physics and advanced fuel cycles, Argonne is exploring new approaches to reduce the long-term hazards associated with used nuclear fuel through research funded by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E).
Used nuclear fuel contains minor actinides and long-lived fission products that can remain hazardous for extended periods, contributing to the challenges of long-term storage. Previous approaches to managing these materials can require complex processes and long-term geological repositories. Finding a way to reduce these long-lived materials could decrease heat and long-term hazards while simplifying requirements for their eventual storage.
To address this challenge, Argonne and its partners are developing NATURE — the Nanofluid-based Accelerator-driven Transmutation Recycler. The concept combines nanoparticles of material from used nuclear fuel suspended in liquid lead with irradiation from a particle accelerator, causing minor actinides to undergo fission and transforming long-lived fission products into shorter-lived ones. A centrifugal separation process then uses differences in mass to separate fission products from the fluid so the process can continue.
Researchers estimate that just a few NATURE systems operating together could process the entire U.S. minor actinide stockpile within 30 years. Over the course of a three-year ARPA-E-funded project, Argonne and partners at Brookhaven National Laboratory, the University of Michigan, MIT, the University of California, Berkeley, and Virginia Tech will use advanced modeling, simulations and experiments to validate the concept, test nanoparticle behavior and demonstrate the separation process.
If successful, NATURE could dramatically reduce the long-term hazards and heat associated with used nuclear fuel while providing a simpler, more cost-effective approach to its management. The technology could ultimately help change how used nuclear fuel is viewed — from a long-term storage challenge to a potential resource for the future.

entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Accelerating Nuclear Fuel Recycling with AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Accelerating Nuclear Fuel Recycling with AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, chemical engineer Bethany Dean-Kersten discusses an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that uses an AI-enabled digital twin to accelerate the development of advanced nuclear fuel recycling facilities.
The United States has more than 90,000 metric tons of used nuclear fuel in storage, and more than 95% of that material could still be used as fuel. As the nation works to expand nuclear energy capacity, recycling used fuel could help strengthen the supply of fuel for advanced reactors. However, designing, building and licensing new recycling facilities can be slow and costly, requiring extensive physical testing before a facility can be built.
To address this challenge, Argonne is working with Case Western Reserve University, Oklo Inc. and ModCon: Transformational AI and Data to develop a digital twin — a dynamic software model — of the first stage of pyroprocessing, a nuclear fuel recycling technology Argonne has advanced for more than two decades. Grounded in chemistry and physics and trained on Argonne experimental data, the model is paired with AI agents that support data preparation, anomaly detection and automated regulatory documentation. This approach could allow engineers to refine facility designs virtually while reducing the need for repeated physical experiments.
The project aims to cut development costs in half, track nuclear material with near-total accuracy and identify potential problems earlier in the development process. By combining Argonne’s expertise in nuclear fuel recycling with AI-enabled modeling, the team is working toward a faster and more cost-effective path for bringing advanced nuclear fuel recycling technologies to commercial deployment. entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Smarter Quantum Sensors Through AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Smarter Quantum Sensors Through AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, physicist Whitney Armstrong discusses an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that is reimagining how superconducting quantum sensors process information.
Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can capture the arrival of individual photons with astonishing timing precision, down to a few trillionths of a second. But turning those signals into usable data typically requires amplification, digitization and conventional computing — steps that can add delays, consume power and discard some of the precise timing information the sensors were designed to capture.
To address this challenge, an Argonne-led team, in partnership with MIT, NIST and Washington University in St. Louis, is working to build computation directly into the superconducting hardware. Their brain-inspired networks use precisely timed electrical pulses traveling through superconducting devices to create coordinated patterns capable of distinguishing incredibly small differences in signal timing, all while operating at the same ultra-cold temperatures as the sensors. AI plays a central role by helping researchers design optimal hardware layouts and train the network’s behavior, while the team is also exploring whether operating the system near a delicate balance between order and chaos can improve performance.
The result could provide a scalable, low-power foundation for processing quantum-sensor information in real time, with potential applications in quantum imaging, sensing and advanced scientific detectors. Learn more about how Argonne is advancing this work under DOE’s Genesis Mission.

entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Protecting Scientific Discovery from Data Tampering with AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Protecting Scientific Discovery from Data Tampering with AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, computer scientist Bogdan Nicolae discusses SPOTTER-AI, an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that uses artificial intelligence to help protect AI-driven scientific research from hidden data tampering.
As scientists increasingly share data, models and workflows to accelerate discovery, ensuring the integrity of those resources becomes increasingly important. Even a small amount of corrupted data could distort an AI model’s results and potentially propagate through other scientific workflows before researchers identify where the problem began. Traditional cybersecurity tools primarily protect computing infrastructure, creating a need for new approaches that can identify manipulation targeting the scientific process itself.
To address this challenge, SPOTTER-AI is being designed to trace the history of the data, models and steps involved in a scientific workflow and identify suspicious activity. The system evaluates whether particular data had an unexpected influence on scientific results, helping distinguish legitimate outliers from potentially manipulated information. If something appears suspicious, an AI agent can trace the problem backward through the workflow to help identify where and how the potential tampering occurred.
Working with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Illinois Institute of Technology, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Exabyte Inc., the Argonne-led team is testing SPOTTER-AI on research that uses artificial intelligence to predict plant traits for bioenergy and agriculture research. The project is developing components as reusable tools for DOE’s Genesis Mission, with the goal of helping researchers maintain confidence in AI-enabled scientific workflows as their use expands. By bringing data provenance, anomaly detection and AI-assisted investigation together, SPOTTER-AI could help protect the integrity of increasingly interconnected scientific discovery.

entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Designing Next-Generation Electronics with AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Designing Next-Generation Electronics with AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, physicist Antonino Miceli discusses CMOS + X, an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that uses artificial intelligence to design and optimize electronics that operate near absolute zero.
Building next-generation electronics for extreme cold requires expertise across multiple fields, including semiconductors, superconductivity, thermal engineering and hardware packaging. This knowledge is often divided among separate teams, tools and scientific disciplines, making it difficult for engineers to understand how a design choice in one area affects performance in another. Testing potential designs can also be slow because predicting how circuits behave at extremely low temperatures often requires time-consuming physics simulations.
To address these challenges, Argonne is leading CMOS + X in partnership with SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, the University of Illinois Chicago and Northwestern University. The project uses a team of AI agents that work together as an autonomous design assistant, building a shared knowledge base, translating designs into testable models and identifying which design choices drive performance. AI surrogate models also replace slower physics simulations with fast predictions of thermal and superconducting behavior, allowing researchers to explore more design possibilities in less time.
By connecting scientific and engineering disciplines that have traditionally been separated, CMOS + X could help researchers design better low-temperature electronics for future applications in quantum sensing and high-precision scientific research. entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Predicting Water Availability and Flood Risk with AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Predicting Water Availability and Flood Risk with AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, geoscientist Eugene Yan discusses an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that uses artificial intelligence to improve predictions of water availability and flood risk across the United States.
Water shortages and flooding pose significant risks to energy production, infrastructure and communities across the country. Yet predicting these risks accurately is difficult: large-scale hydrologic models can be too computationally demanding to capture local detail across an entire continent, while also oversimplifying interactions between surface water and groundwater. Many models also struggle to account for human activities such as groundwater pumping, making it harder to anticipate droughts, floods and changing water demands.
To address these challenges, Argonne is leading a team that includes Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Princeton University, the University of Arizona, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Georgia Institute of Technology and Cognition AI to develop a new AI foundation model. The model will learn from physics-based simulations at multiple scales, combining continental, regional and local information to improve predictions of groundwater levels, soil moisture, streamflow and flood hazards. The system is also designed to incorporate real-time observations and estimate forecast uncertainty without requiring computationally expensive retraining.
The team will initially focus on water availability and flood risks in the Midwest, with the goal of scaling the approach into a high-resolution, AI-driven water forecasting system for the continental United States. The technology could give communities, energy providers and other decision-makers better tools to anticipate water shortages, manage flood risks and strengthen the resilience of energy systems. Learn more about how Argonne is advancing this work under DOE’s Genesis Mission.

entry.title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Reimagining Nuclear Reactor Design with AI

media:group.media:title: DOE’s Genesis Mission: Reimagining Nuclear Reactor Design with AI
media:group.media:description:
Argonne National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center where scientists and engineers pioneer breakthroughs that address some of the world’s most pressing challenges. In this video, senior nuclear engineer Rick Vilim discusses Prometheus, an Argonne-led project under DOE’s Genesis Mission that combines artificial intelligence with advanced nuclear expertise to accelerate the design and deployment of nuclear reactors.
As demand for electricity grows, deploying new nuclear power at the pace and scale needed to help meet the nation’s energy needs remains a significant challenge. Nuclear projects involve complex design, licensing, manufacturing, construction and operating processes, with critical information often passing among many people and systems. These bottlenecks can slow decision-making and make it difficult to carry knowledge and lessons learned from one project into the next.
To address these challenges, Prometheus is developing an AI-enabled platform designed to make information and expertise more accessible throughout the nuclear reactor lifecycle. AI agents could help engineering teams share design changes, support licensing reviews using previous regulatory information, monitor construction and manufacturing, and assist with routine plant operations. Rather than removing people from the process, Prometheus keeps humans in the loop while using AI to help experts work more efficiently and make informed decisions faster.
The Argonne-led team includes national laboratories, universities and industry partners working together to move advances in AI-enabled nuclear engineering toward real-world applications. The project has already demonstrated AI control of a simulated reactor and installed AI-designed hardware in an active test reactor, while pursuing ambitious goals for reducing design, licensing, manufacturing and deployment timelines.
By combining artificial intelligence with decades of nuclear science and engineering expertise, Prometheus aims to help make nuclear technology faster and more efficient to design and deploy. Working closely with industry is central to that mission, helping translate research advances into technologies that can strengthen U.S. nuclear capabilities, support growing electricity demand and contribute to economic growth.
